cards.q: What is an IPv6 link-local address?
cards.a: A link-local address (prefix fe80::/10) is automatically configured on every IPv6 interface. It is mandatory, non-routable, and used locally for ND, SLAAC signaling, neighbor discovery, and routing protocol adjacencies.

cards.q: Are link-local addresses ever forwarded by routers?
cards.a: No. Link-local scope is the link only, so routers never forward them and they are never advertised into the global routing table.

cards.q: How is a link-local address generated?
cards.a: Either from the MAC via EUI-64 (flip the U/L bit and insert fffe) or randomly/stable per RFC 7217. It is always present, added automatically by ipv6 enable, and unique per interface.

cards.q: Why does pinging a link-local address require a zone identifier?
cards.a: Because fe80:: addresses are identical on every host, the scope is per-link and you must identify the interface: ping6 fe80::1%eth0 on Linux/macOS and ping fe80::1%5 on Windows.

cards.q: What protocols and functions rely on link-local addresses?
cards.a: Neighbor Discovery (NS/NA, RS/RA), SLAAC unicast, routing protocol adjacencies such as OSPFv3 and EIGRPv6 which use fe80 as next hop, default gateway learning from the RA sender, and management reachability on the connected segment.

cards.q: What is the lifetime of each IPv6 address type on an interface?
cards.a: Link-local is mandatory and never removed; GUA/ULA addresses are removed when SLAAC stops receiving Router Advertisements or when their lifetime expires; temporary privacy addresses rotate every few days.

cards.q: How do you enable link-local addressing on a Cisco IOS interface?
cards.a: Use ipv6 enable to auto-generate a fe80::/64 address with no global address, or ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local for a manual, deterministic link-local address.

cards.q: What commands verify link-local addresses on Cisco IOS?
cards.a: show ipv6 interface Gi0/1 | include Link|fe80 and ping6 fe80::1%0 to ping from the device itself using the zone.

cards.q: Is a fe80::/10 address invalid or broken?
cards.a: No. It is a normal, mandatory link-local address; this is the most common misunderstanding behind 'why do I have this weird fe80 address'.

cards.q: Can a link-local address appear in the global routing table or be pinged across routers?
cards.a: No. Link-local is not routable, so it never appears in a global routing table and pinging one across routers fails.

cards.q: Why is the % zone id in fe80::1%eth0 significant?
cards.a: The zone id %interface is required to disambiguate which interface the link-local address belongs to when multiple interfaces exist.

cards.q: Can a link-local address appear as a next hop in an IPv6 routing table?
cards.a: Yes. On point-to-point links the next hop may display as a fe80 link-local address.

cards.q: Is a link-local fe80 address the IPv6 equivalent of IPv4 APIPA (169.254)?
cards.a: No. fe80 is normal and deliberate in IPv6, unlike IPv4's 169.254 APIPA fallback that indicates DHCP failure.
